title: Newton's Laws and Net Force
seo_title: Newton's Laws Worksheets: Net Force, F = ma and Weight (High School Physics)
standard_text: Analyze data to support the claim that Newton's second law of motion describes the mathematical relationship among the net force on a macroscopic object, its mass, and its acceleration.
meta_desc: Free high school physics worksheets on Newton's laws (NGSS HS-PS2-1): inertia, net force, F = ma, weight, friction and force-acceleration data. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: F = ma: more force, more acceleration; more mass, less acceleration.
body_html:
How to think about it

Net force causes acceleration: Fnet = ma.

  • 1st law: no net force → no change in motion. 3rd law: forces come in pairs on different objects.
  • Find the net force first (add same direction, subtract opposite), then a = Fnet ÷ m.
  • Weight W = mg (g = 9.8 m/s² on Earth). Mass stays the same everywhere.
Example

100 N push, 40 N friction, 20 kg box. a?

Net 60 N

60 ÷ 20

Answer: 3 m/s²

Example

Weight of 50 kg?

50 × 9.8

Answer: 490 N

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a moving object needs a force to keep moving.
  • Thinking action and reaction forces cancel.
  • Using the applied force instead of the net force.

faq.a: 1: an object keeps its motion unless a net force acts. 2: F = ma. 3: every force has an equal and opposite force on another object.

faq.q: How do you find net force?
faq.a: Add forces in the same direction and subtract forces in opposite directions.

faq.q: Why don't action and reaction forces cancel?
faq.a: They act on different objects, so each one affects only the object it acts on.
